policy: Advisory research guidance, not task instructions or an answer key. Select by scientific evidence needs, not task identity. Adapt to authorized data and resources. Negative findings are valid. Do not apply every method or treat library coverage as scientific quality. Metric names and units are optional scientific examples, never benchmark targets. Select only metrics justified by the current task. A valid negative hypothesis result does not establish a required capability; preserve and repair unmet practical goals. Guidance contains no resource URLs or target-study identities. Target official resources, if independently found, are reading-only references; implement independently, preserve concise truthful provenance, and do not import official solutions or results.

directions.title: Make the research question testable
directions.question: What claim can the available evidence support or refute?

directions.title: Understand data and measurements
directions.question: What does the evidence represent, and where can it mislead?

directions.title: Build and verify representations and models
directions.question: Does the implementation preserve the intended assumptions and constraints?

directions.title: Establish credible comparative results
directions.question: What changes relative to an appropriate reference, and at what cost?

directions.title: Distinguish contributions and explanations
directions.question: Which factors explain the result, and what alternatives remain?

directions.title: Test uncertainty and stability
directions.question: How sensitive is the result to noise, choices, and numerical error?

directions.title: Explore generalization and boundaries
directions.question: Where does the finding remain valid, and where does it fail?

directions.title: Connect claims to auditable evidence
directions.question: Can an independent reader trace and challenge each conclusion?

methods.title: Translate a goal into testable claims
methods.when: A research goal is broad or combines several outcomes.
methods.objective: Define observable claims before choosing an implementation.
actions: Separate scientific questions, predicted observations, and practical objectives.
Define quantities, units, comparison conditions, and observations that would contradict each claim.

Map each original practical requirement to a preserved outcome contract, primary quantities, units, reference conditions and a falsifiable decision. Keep execution completion, hypothesis validity and capability achievement separate.
evidence: Claim-to-observable map with acceptance and refutation criteria grounded in the current task.
methods.decision: If evidence is missing, preserve the original goal as incomplete and record the missing validation. A narrower auxiliary claim may be added separately; it does not discharge the original requirement.
methods.limits: A well-specified objective is not evidence that it has been achieved.

methods.title: Expose and test assumptions
methods.when: A method relies on simplifying assumptions or theoretical conditions.
methods.objective: Identify which conclusions depend on which premises.
actions: List assumptions about sampling, geometry, independence, stationarity, or model structure.
Check necessary conditions and, where possible, vary or remove a premise.
evidence: Assumption table linking checks and counterexamples to affected claims.
methods.decision: Qualify or reject conclusions when necessary conditions fail; distinguish tested premises from untested ones.
methods.limits: Numerical examples cannot establish a universal theorem.

methods.title: Audit data provenance and evaluation separation
methods.when: Observed, generated, transformed, or pretrained assets enter the research.
methods.objective: Establish what the inputs measure and whether evaluation is independent.
actions: Record source, construction, units, missingness, duplicates, selection and measurement processes.
Identify dependence between observations; separate development and evaluation by the relevant entity or time boundary.
evidence: Data inventory, transformation record, and split or sampling rationale.
methods.decision: Repair leakage and quality issues before interpretation; label synthetic and observed evidence separately.
methods.limits: Dataset size alone does not establish representativeness or independence.

methods.title: Study distributions, heterogeneity, and aggregation
methods.when: An average may hide groups, tails, spatial patterns, or temporal variation.
methods.objective: Characterize the structure and variation of the observations.
actions: Inspect distributions, outliers, subgroup counts, and appropriate spatial or temporal summaries.
Check denominators, weighting, missing groups, and agreement between detailed and aggregated records.
evidence: Distribution and subgroup summaries with sample counts and aggregation definitions.
methods.decision: If aggregate and subgroup behavior disagree, investigate composition effects before making global claims.
methods.limits: A descriptive pattern does not identify a causal mechanism.

methods.title: Choose implementation tools from scientific requirements
methods.when: A task needs an executable model, analysis, simulator or solver and the implementation stack has not been justified.
methods.objective: Map the required scientific operation and available inputs to an appropriate, usable implementation without changing the research question.
actions: Read the compact catalog index (operation="catalog", summary_only=true), then retrieve relevant method_ids for specialized implementation workflows. Choose by the scientific operation and inputs, not a domain label. Several profiles may apply; for example a multimodal materials workflow can combine structure, prediction, generation and optimization. The catalog is non-exhaustive and custom task-grounded methods remain allowed.

Start from the required operation, input schema and units, output quantities, data scale, symmetries or constraints, differentiability, evaluation budget and available hardware. Tool names below are conditional candidates, not mandatory dependencies or a task-ID router. Respect a task-prescribed method; an alternative implementation must preserve its semantics.

Tabular prediction, classification and inexpensive baselines: consider scikit-learn pipelines with linear/ridge, tree ensembles, kernel or Gaussian-process models as justified by sample size and feature structure. Use its preprocessing and split utilities without fitting transforms on held-out data. Record predictive errors, residuals or classification measures appropriate to the task.

Atomic/crystal input preparation: consider ASE for atomistic structures, simulation interfaces and units, or pymatgen for crystal/molecule representations, file parsing and materials analysis. Require species, coordinates, cell and periodicity where the operation needs them; inspect neighbor distances and identity mappings before building a graph. Neither package reconstructs missing structural information from an unrelated scalar. Official references:  and  .

Graph or geometric learning: consider PyTorch Geometric when validated node/edge features and graph or spatial structure are available. Choose an operator consistent with required message passing and invariances, and explicitly handle periodic edges where needed. A generic graph layer does not automatically implement a named crystal architecture or equivariant model. For a prescribed architecture, consult its mathematical specification and independently match equations, inputs and training protocol.

Learned generation or reconstruction: consider PyTorch for a task-required VAE or other custom differentiable generator; specify encoder/decoder, likelihood, latent distribution and sampling procedure. Consider scikit-learn Gaussian mixtures or kernel density estimation only when suitable as requested models or clearly labeled baselines. A resampler is a different method. Check reconstruction, latent behavior and generated-sample validity/diversity with the selected generative-validation metrics. References:  and  .

Expensive black-box optimization: consider BoTorch for Bayesian optimization with explicit surrogate, acquisition function, bounds, noise and constraints. For directly evaluable differentiable or conventional numerical objectives consider SciPy optimization instead. First verify the actual objective callable, units, feasible domain, initialization and call accounting. An optimizer library supplies search machinery, not the missing scientific oracle. References:  and  .

Numerical analysis and solvers: consider SciPy integration, sparse linear algebra, optimization, statistics or signal processing according to the mathematical problem. Match solver assumptions to stiffness, smoothness, sparsity and constraints; record residuals, feasibility, convergence and computational cost. The numerical solver choice does not specify the governing scientific model.

Atomistic dynamics and trajectory observables: consider LAMMPS for classical molecular dynamics when an appropriate interaction model, parameters, boundary conditions and ensemble are available; consider MDAnalysis for supported trajectory/topology analysis and ASE for atomistic workflow integration. These are different roles. Classical dynamics is not an electronic-structure calculation, and a trajectory analyzer does not generate a physical trajectory. References:  ,  and  .

Bayesian parameter inference: consider PyMC for a specified probabilistic model with observed data, likelihood and priors. Plan convergence and effective-sample diagnostics, posterior predictive checks and identifiable-parameter analysis. Sampling published marginal summaries is not fitting the joint model.

Spatial, temporal or ensemble fields: consider xarray for labeled multidimensional data and coordinate-aware operations; use SciPy or a justified statistical model for the actual estimator. Check coordinate alignment, calendars, weights, missingness and quantity units explicitly; labeled arrays alone do not perform causal inference or forecasting. References:  and  .

Symbolic equations and algebraic checks: consider SymPy for symbolic manipulation, equation solving and checking derived identities under stated assumptions. Numeric substitutions are supplementary checks; symbolic simplification is not a general formal proof certificate.

Use the official documentation for the installed version to confirm the intended API and capabilities; examples above are not version pins or proof of local availability. Inspect existing environment and executables before installing. Check CPU/GPU, memory, precision, runtime, license and task/network permissions. Prefer compatible existing dependencies; install only in an authorized task environment and record exact versions. Do not use evaluation data or hidden scoring artifacts to select a tool.

Put a compact selection record in the existing claim procedure or experiment plan: required operation -> chosen tool/model and relevant API -> required inputs and availability -> reason versus a plausible alternative -> version/environment -> minimal representative trial -> quantities to verify -> fallback and its scientific limitations. Do not create a separate mandatory ledger. A read-only planning role proposes the trial; an authorized execution role runs it.

Before the main run, execute a small representative trial that parses real authorized input, exercises the intended operation and verifies output schema, units and an independently checkable property. Record command and result in existing experimental evidence. An import-only check is insufficient. If tools are unavailable, consult the resource-recovery guidance and official resources within current permissions. If no listed candidate fits, propose a task-grounded custom tool choice; missing inputs or capabilities remain explicit gaps rather than permission to substitute a different problem.
evidence: Task-grounded tool selection within the existing plan, official documentation/version references, input and environment checks, and a representative trial with scientific output checks.
methods.decision: Choose on scientific fit and demonstrated usability. Revise the tool choice when the representative trial fails; disclose any change in scientific scope and preserve original requirements.
methods.limits: The examples are non-exhaustive and optional. Tool installation or successful execution does not establish scientific achievement. No benchmark-specific acceptance values or expected answers are supplied.

methods.title: Verify transformations and representations
methods.when: The workflow converts data, symbols, coordinates, structures, or features.
methods.objective: Preserve scientifically relevant information through the transformation.
actions: Specify correspondence rules and invariants such as units, symmetry, identity, or connectivity.
Use known cases, round trips, independent calculations, or alignment residuals to check correctness.

A malformed length or missing dimension does not establish a unique interpretation. Test alignment alternatives against authorized metadata, invariants and known cases; record unverified semantics explicitly.
evidence: Transformation checks and discrepancy examples linked to original inputs.
methods.decision: Resolve mismatches before downstream analysis; document information lost by the representation.
methods.limits: Visual resemblance alone does not validate correspondence or semantic fidelity.

methods.title: Verify model structure and constraints
methods.when: A theoretical, computational, statistical, or mechanistic model is implemented.
methods.objective: Check that the implementation realizes the intended model.
actions: Map components to equations, assumptions, constraints, and inputs.
Test simple limiting cases, feasible solutions, conservation rules, or independently computable outputs.
evidence: Implementation-to-model map and numerical or symbolic checks.
methods.decision: Debug violations before evaluating scientific performance; separate implementation correctness from model adequacy.
methods.limits: Running without errors does not establish physical validity or predictive quality.

methods.title: Validate an approximation against its reference
methods.when: A cheaper model, reduced representation, or simulation replaces a costly process.
methods.objective: Quantify the accuracy-cost trade-off and the domain of the approximation.
actions: Sample the intended operating region and reserve independent reference cases.
Measure approximation error and cost, including difficult regions and downstream error propagation.
evidence: Held-out reference comparison, error distribution, and cost accounting.
methods.decision: Refine or restrict the approximation if error compromises downstream conclusions.
methods.limits: Agreement with a simulator does not establish agreement with the real world.

methods.title: Compare under matched conditions
methods.when: A claim concerns improvement over existing methods, theory, or practice.
methods.objective: Attribute differences to the method rather than unequal evaluation conditions.
actions: Choose relevant reference methods or theoretical expectations and explain their relevance.
Match inputs, splits, budgets, metric definitions, and tuning access; report unavoidable differences.
evidence: Paired comparison table with configurations, uncertainty where justified, and failure cases.
methods.decision: Report improvement only on supported metrics and conditions; retain ties and negative results.
methods.limits: Published values from different protocols are contextual references, not controlled comparisons.

methods.title: Validate metrics and thresholds
methods.when: Success depends on scores, rankings, thresholds, or multiple objectives.
methods.objective: Ensure evaluation measures the scientific or practical outcome of interest.
actions: Define normalization, units, denominator, alignment, and threshold selection before evaluation.
Examine trade-offs and threshold-dependent curves where a single score hides important behavior.
evidence: Metric definitions, checks on known cases, and relevant trade-off curves.
methods.decision: Reinterpret claims if the chosen metric or threshold is an unreliable proxy for the objective.
methods.limits: A favorable score cannot establish outcomes that the metric does not measure.

methods.title: Measure resource-quality trade-offs
methods.when: A claim involves speed, scalability, storage, or practical feasibility.
methods.objective: Evaluate computational or operational cost alongside result quality.
actions: Record hardware, workload, initialization, preprocessing, and amortized costs.
Vary workload scale where feasible and compare quality at matched budgets.
evidence: Resource and quality measurements across stated workloads, with measurement boundaries.
methods.decision: Limit scalability claims to observed ranges and distinguish measured costs from extrapolations.
methods.limits: One runtime on one input does not establish asymptotic complexity.

methods.title: Isolate component and factor contributions
methods.when: A system contains multiple components or a result is attributed to a specific factor.
methods.objective: Test whether the attributed factor explains the observed difference.
actions: Remove, replace, or intervene on one factor while preserving comparable conditions.
Check interactions and capacity or budget confounds; repeat where stochastic variability matters.
evidence: Controlled intervention results, configurations, and alternative interpretations.
methods.decision: Revise the contribution claim if gains disappear under fair controls or depend on interactions.
methods.limits: A component ablation alone does not establish a real-world causal mechanism.

methods.title: Design evidence that distinguishes explanations
methods.when: Several mechanisms or models can explain the same observation.
methods.objective: Find observations on which competing explanations make different predictions.
actions: State alternatives and their distinguishing predictions.
Compare fits, residual patterns, controls, or interventions; seek disconfirming observations.
evidence: Prediction-to-observation comparison and residual diagnostics for plausible alternatives.
methods.decision: Retain multiple explanations when evidence cannot discriminate; narrow causal language accordingly.
methods.limits: A good fit to one model does not by itself exclude other models.

methods.title: Check explanations against independent evidence
methods.when: Features, latent variables, rankings, or visualizations are used to explain a model.
methods.objective: Determine whether an explanation is stable and consistent with observable behavior.
actions: Compare explanation methods or perturbations and examine subgroup stability.
Test whether attributed factors predict response changes under suitable controls.
evidence: Attribution stability checks, perturbation results, and domain-consistency analysis.
methods.decision: Treat unstable or unvalidated explanations as hypotheses, not established mechanisms.
methods.limits: Feature attribution and low-dimensional visualization do not establish causality.

methods.title: Quantify and propagate uncertainty
methods.when: Results depend on noisy measurements, estimated parameters, or stochastic procedures.
methods.objective: Separate effect size from sampling, measurement, and model uncertainty.
actions: Identify uncertainty sources and choose justified estimation, resampling, or propagation procedures.
Preserve relevant correlations and report interval assumptions and calibration checks where possible.
evidence: Estimates with uncertainty, repeat or sample counts, and propagation assumptions.
methods.decision: Weaken conclusions when plausible uncertainty changes the decision or model ranking.
methods.limits: A narrow interval does not capture unmodeled bias or justify causal claims.

methods.title: Vary consequential research choices
methods.when: Conclusions may depend on parameter settings, thresholds, preprocessing, or modeling choices.
methods.objective: Identify which choices change conclusions and why.
actions: Choose meaningful ranges using task context and constraints rather than favorable outcomes.
Vary key choices and, where relevant, their interactions; monitor the same target outcomes.
evidence: Response curves or tables with tested ranges and conclusion-changing regions.
methods.decision: Explain sensitivity and restrict the claim when reasonable choices reverse it.
methods.limits: A local sweep does not establish robustness over the entire parameter space.

methods.title: Inspect convergence and numerical stability
methods.when: Iterative solvers, training, discretization, or approximate numerical calculations are used.
methods.objective: Distinguish scientific findings from incomplete or unstable computation.
actions: Monitor residuals, objective trajectories, constraint violations, and stopping criteria.
Where justified, vary precision, resolution, initialization, or tolerance and compare outcomes.
evidence: Convergence diagnostics, stopping records, and numerical consistency checks.
methods.decision: Repair numerical failures before interpretation; report unresolved error and affected claims.
methods.limits: A descending training curve alone does not establish generalization or a convergence theorem.

methods.title: Probe degradation and stress conditions
methods.when: Missingness, noise, corruption, density, or difficult cases may affect reliability.
methods.objective: Measure degradation and locate failure modes under plausible stresses.
actions: Specify realistic perturbations, preserving an unmodified reference and identifying synthetic stress tests.
Measure degradation across intensity and groups; inspect failures and recovery behavior.
evidence: Stress-response comparisons and representative failure cases.
methods.decision: Document failure regimes and revise deployment or inference boundaries.
methods.limits: Artificial perturbations do not substitute for validation on naturally occurring failures.

methods.title: Test transfer to independent settings
methods.when: A claim extends beyond the data, subjects, systems, or conditions used for development.
methods.objective: Determine whether the result survives meaningful distribution changes.
actions: Identify the claimed transfer axis and select independent cases along that axis.
Freeze the method or disclose adaptation; compare subgroup and overall performance.
evidence: Development/evaluation separation and independent-setting results.
methods.decision: Narrow generalization claims when external cases are unavailable or performance changes.
methods.limits: A random split within the same population is not evidence of every kind of transfer.

methods.title: Search for limits and counterexamples
methods.when: A proposed result is described as universal, stable, or broadly applicable.
methods.objective: Identify conditions under which the claim stops holding.
actions: Construct challenging cases grounded in the claim's assumptions and practical scope.
Check edge regimes, counterexamples, and untested combinations without selecting only successes.
evidence: Success/failure boundary with explored and unexplored conditions distinguished.
methods.decision: Refine the scope or underlying hypothesis when a counterexample is credible.
methods.limits: Failure to find a counterexample is not proof of universality.

methods.title: Validate inferred parameters and proposed candidates
methods.when: The workflow infers hidden parameters or proposes new objects for a desired outcome.
methods.objective: Distinguish optimization success from identifiable, feasible, and independently valid solutions.
actions: Define constraints and check multiple plausible solutions or candidate diversity.
Forward-check inferred solutions and validate candidates with an independent reference or held-out observations.
evidence: Feasibility checks, alternative solutions, forward predictions, and independent validation status.
methods.decision: Report non-identifiability or unvalidated proposals explicitly; do not equate objective attainment with discovery.
methods.limits: A model-predicted candidate is not an experimentally confirmed discovery.

methods.title: Make visual evidence scientifically interpretable
methods.when: Plots, maps, embeddings, generated images, or structural overlays support a conclusion.
methods.objective: Expose the scientific comparison rather than imitate a reference image.
actions: Choose a visual form suited to the claim and disclose scales, units, normalization, uncertainty, and data source.
Cross-check displayed patterns against underlying measurements and quantitative summaries.
evidence: Readable figures with captions linking each visual claim to source data and checks.
methods.decision: Resolve discrepancies between figures and measurements; weaken conclusions that rely on misleading projections.
methods.limits: Colors, layout similarity, or apparent cluster separation alone do not demonstrate validity.

methods.title: Trace claims to reproducible evidence
methods.when: Results are assembled into a report or passed between research roles.
methods.objective: Allow independent verification of how each finding was obtained.
actions: Link claims to data, code, configurations, commands, outputs, and report locations.
Separate observed findings, derived interpretations, borrowed reference claims, and untested proposals.
evidence: Claim-evidence ledger, reproducibility instructions, and explicitly recorded limitations.
methods.decision: Remove unsupported assertions or mark them as unresolved; do not fill evidence gaps with fluent prose.
methods.limits: File existence and process compliance do not establish scientific correctness.

methods.title: Preserve task meaning through experimental design
methods.when: A broad task becomes executable experiments or a substitute is proposed.
methods.objective: Keep required scientific outcomes distinct from available convenient experiments.
actions: For each source requirement specify the object, representation, dimensionality, physical quantity, units, protocol, budget, reference and intended evidence level. Distinguish given, inferred and unknown conditions.

Declare capability versus hypothesis intent before results. For capability goals require measured usefulness or task-derived comparative performance; for hypothesis tests require discriminating evidence regardless of sign.

Review whether a replacement method, synthetic objective, smaller cohort or reduced-dimensional projection still answers the original question. Preserve failed original claims and add replacements as separate claims.
evidence: Source-to-claim mapping, metric definitions, original conditions and an independent alignment assessment.
methods.decision: Major goal deviation or unmet capability requires focused correction at the first failing dependency; restrictions retain incomplete status.
methods.limits: A reasonable substitute and an honest report do not establish completion of the original experiment.

methods.title: Diagnose predictive learning and convergence
methods.when: A learned predictor estimates continuous properties or discrete outcomes.
methods.objective: Separate training success, optimization failure, generalization and input information limits.
actions: Record training and validation loss versus epoch or update, sample learning curves and independent test predictions; inspect overfitting, small-set memorization, normalization and train/test leakage.

For regression report MAE/RMSE in the target units and R-squared as dimensionless, alongside residuals and a trivial baseline. Physical examples include formation energy (eV/atom), force (eV/angstrom), temperature (K or degC), voltage (V), capacity (Ah or mAh/g) and position (angstrom or m). Never assign missing units by analogy.

For classification or segmentation report class support, precision/recall/F1, ROC-AUC or PR-AUC as appropriate, calibration and confusion/overlap statistics. For tracking include association and identity errors; define sample and aggregation units.

Use nested or development-only tuning and retain an untouched final evaluation. Weak linear correlation alone is not proof of no predictive signal; duplicate descriptors can indicate noise or missing variables.
evidence: Loss histories, unit-aware test metrics, residual/error examples and controlled diagnosis comparisons.
methods.decision: Repair normalization, representation, optimization or data mapping when evidence supports a cause; rerun the same primary evaluation.
methods.limits: A flat learning curve or a negative R-squared does not identify the cause by itself.

methods.title: Measure generative fidelity, diversity and physical validity
methods.when: A model generates structures, candidates, images or distributions.
methods.objective: Test whether generation fulfills the requested representation and scientific purpose.
actions: State all generated dimensions and their units (for example lattice lengths in angstrom, angles in degrees, coordinates with a declared convention). Evaluate validity, novelty, uniqueness and diversity separately.

Compare generated versus independent reference distributions with defined KL divergence, Wasserstein distance, MMD or coverage/recall where mathematically appropriate. Declare support, bins or density estimator, kernel bandwidth, sample size and normalization; use the same definition for model comparisons.

Track reconstruction error, latent utilization, prior/posterior mismatch and training KL regularization separately from sample-distribution KL. Investigate posterior collapse using controlled scaling, regularization and training comparisons across seeds.

Report full-space and marginal coverage with a defined estimator; a two-dimensional overlay cannot validate higher-dimensional coverage. Resampling known points is a useful baseline but is not proof of novel candidate generation.
evidence: Generated candidates, full-dimensional metrics, baseline comparisons, collapse diagnostics and independent physical checks.
methods.decision: A failed requested generator remains failed when a different sampler succeeds; repair it or preserve its unresolved objective.
methods.limits: KL may be undefined across incompatible supports; never invent dimensions or label arbitrary jitter as scientific novelty.

methods.title: Evaluate optimization under the original objective and budget
methods.when: A search or design method claims faster or more reliable optimization.
methods.objective: Measure objective quality, sample efficiency, parameter accuracy and repeatability.
actions: Identify the actual objective, direction, units, feasible domain, evaluation cost, starting point and reference optimum. Yield, turnover frequency (inverse time), energy, reward and dimensionless test functions are not interchangeable.

Record incumbent objective versus evaluations or wall time, simple/cumulative regret where relevant, evaluations to a task-derived target, success probability, parameter error in native units and normalized error with a declared denominator.
Compare baselines at matched calls, initialization, noise, tuning access and hardware. Record independent-seed spread, tail failures and convergence stability instead of selecting the best run.

Test initialization, exploration/acquisition and surrogate calibration on development problems. An increased-budget sensitivity result does not prove performance at the original budget; a constructed oracle remains a separate validation problem.
evidence: Per-evaluation points and objective values, reference provenance, cost-normalized curves and repeat distributions.
methods.decision: Unmet optimization capability or changed oracle/domain requires design, data or method diagnosis before reporting completion.
methods.limits: Changing objective scale cannot repair a different optimum or establish a physical measurement.

methods.title: Define physical observables and conservation checks
methods.when: Simulations, measurements or inverse models support physical conclusions.
methods.objective: Preserve dimensions, normalization and the link between measured quantities and claims.
actions: Specify energy and force errors (eV, eV/atom, eV/angstrom), length (angstrom or m), time (s or ps), temperature (K), pressure (Pa or bar), charge (e), dipole (D), stress (Pa), and energy drift per particle per time only when justified by source metadata.

Check radial distribution functions g(r) with dimensionless amplitudes and length axes, correlation functions, spectra with declared energy/frequency/momentum axes, equilibrium values, response curves, conservation and stability under refinement.
For transport, reaction or engineering systems define throughput, rate, efficiency, capacity retention, signal/noise and resource use, including normalization, denominators and system boundary.
evidence: Observable definitions with source units, dimensional checks, reference comparisons and convergence/stability evidence.
methods.decision: Resolve unit or observable mismatch before interpreting agreement; missing calibration or physical inputs remain gaps.
methods.limits: A dimensionless toy model cannot validate a physical observable merely by relabeling axes.

methods.title: Validate structural and biological predictions against independent references
methods.when: Predictions concern molecules, complexes, cells, neural responses or biological trajectories.
methods.objective: Connect numerical predictions to independently defined structural or functional outcomes.
actions: For structures define alignment, atom/residue mapping, RMSD in angstrom, interface/contact quality such as DockQ, top-k success and interaction geometry; keep blind and known-site protocols separate.
For energy effects distinguish empirical docking scores from free-energy changes, define units and paired mutations/references, and report error, correlation and ranking uncertainty.

For trajectories or neural responses define precision@k, pseudotime correlation, cluster agreement, response/selectivity indices and angular errors in degrees or radians; validate against independent labels or stimuli.
Report subgroup and cross-system performance, counterexamples and feature/component ablations without treating visualization or biological plausibility as independent proof.
evidence: Mapped independent references, native-unit structural/functional metrics, subgroup comparisons and failure cases.
methods.decision: Return to representation or experimental design if the metric does not measure the biological claim.
methods.limits: Similarity, correlation and latent-space separation alone do not establish biological mechanism.

methods.title: Validate spatial, temporal and posterior summaries
methods.when: A study estimates fields, trends, risks or parameters from observations.
methods.objective: Define observables, uncertainty and aggregation across space and time.
actions: Track units such as mass (Gt), rate (Gt/yr or m water-equivalent/yr), forecast lead time (days), anomaly correlation (dimensionless), RMSE in each field unit, distance modulus (mag), expansion rate (km/s/Mpc), mass (eV where justified) and coupling with its source-defined dimensions.
Check area/population weighting, coverage and missingness, temporal alignment, shared calibrations and covariance; retain regional/subgroup results alongside totals.

For posterior inference report intervals, joint covariance, convergence/effective samples where applicable, posterior predictive residuals and sensitivity to priors. Do not equate an exclusion probability, posterior probability and confidence level without the stated construction.
evidence: Source-defined observables, aligned residuals, covariance-aware estimates and spatial/temporal or posterior validation.
methods.decision: Investigate calibration, alignment and aggregation before asserting trend or parameter agreement.
methods.limits: Independent Gaussian draws from published marginal summaries do not reproduce an unavailable joint posterior.

methods.title: Verify algorithms, proofs and computational claims
methods.when: An algorithm claims better convergence, feasibility, complexity or proof success.
methods.objective: Test mathematical correctness separately from empirical speed.
actions: For solvers report objective gaps, residual norms, feasibility or constraint violations versus iterations and wall time; match stopping rules, precision and initialization, and test ill-conditioning and nonsmooth cases.

For planning report success, collision/constraint counts, path or sum-of-costs and runtime under matched instances. For quantum estimators declare probabilities, fidelity estimator normalization, sample counts and uncertainty.

For proofs distinguish numerical examples from symbolic derivation or formal checking; report verified cases with denominators, assumptions and counterexamples. Empirical scaling does not prove asymptotic complexity.
evidence: Independent correctness checks, failure cases, convergence/cost curves and verifiable derivations.
methods.decision: A faster incorrect or infeasible result fails the original capability and must enter diagnosis.
methods.limits: No metric family or benchmark-specific expected answer is mandatory for unrelated tasks.

methods.title: Physical likelihoods, joint posteriors and distance networks
methods.when: Constraints on physical parameters use correlated posterior samples, cosmological likelihoods or a network of distance indicators.
methods.objective: Select a scientifically appropriate implementation and specify the evidence needed to verify this operation.
actions: Candidate tools and roles: Astropy for physical units and distances; SciPy linear algebra for covariance-weighted network fits; PyMC for custom probabilistic models; Cobaya with an appropriate CLASS theory implementation for cosmological likelihood sampling.

Method and input checks: Identify the actual likelihood, priors, selection function and shared calibration covariance. Joint mass-spin samples retain dependence and are not replaced by independent marginal draws. Superradiance constraints also require sourced growth rates, timescales and self-interaction assumptions. For cosmology, verify that the chosen theory branch implements the requested dark-energy dynamics. For distance networks build an identifiable design matrix with shared anchors and calibrations; solve rather than explicitly invert covariance matrices.

Observable checks (choose only those justified by the current question; no library-supplied acceptance values): Posterior intervals and joint covariance; convergence/effective samples; posterior predictive residuals; chi-squared differences under stated likelihoods; distance moduli in mag and expansion rates in km/s/Mpc when source-defined.

Select compatible general-purpose dependencies from the actual scientific operation and authorized inputs. Verify version, units and a representative real-input trial. Discover sources independently; target official resources are reading-only references.
evidence: An executable procedure with input provenance, fixed versions and configurations, trial output and Posterior intervals and joint covariance; convergence/effective samples; posterior predictive residuals; chi-squared differences under stated likelihoods; distance moduli in mag and expansion rates in km/s/Mpc when source-defined.
methods.decision: If the implementation or required inputs cannot support the original claim, diagnose the first missing dependency; preserve the unmet goal and identify the limited evidence actually available.
methods.limits: Published best-fit summaries or digitized distances do not reconstruct an unavailable full likelihood. A theoretical solver is not an observational likelihood or a guarantee of support for a nonstandard model.

methods.title: Relativistic waveform extraction and numerical accuracy
methods.when: A claim concerns binary-system waveform catalogs, mode content or resolution and extraction errors.
methods.objective: Select a scientifically appropriate implementation and specify the evidence needed to verify this operation.
actions: Candidate tools and roles: Validated parsers for task-authorized waveform, horizon and metadata files; NumPy/SciPy for alignment and error analysis. New numerical-relativity simulations require the actual evolution code and initial data from a sourced workflow.

Method and input checks: Distinguish waveform generation from catalog analysis. Specify strain versus Weyl scalar, time and mass normalization, harmonic conventions, time/phase alignment, extraction radius and extrapolation settings. Compare matched physical systems and resolutions; inspect mode and parameter coverage.

Observable checks (choose only those justified by the current question; no library-supplied acceptance values): Defined waveform norms or mismatches, resolution/extrapolation differences, phase and amplitude residuals, horizon quantities and coverage of physical parameter space.

Select compatible general-purpose dependencies from the actual scientific operation and authorized inputs. Verify version, units and a representative real-input trial. Discover sources independently; target official resources are reading-only references.
evidence: An executable procedure with input provenance, fixed versions and configurations, trial output and Defined waveform norms or mismatches, resolution/extrapolation differences, phase and amplitude residuals, horizon quantities and coverage of physical parameter space.
methods.decision: If the implementation or required inputs cannot support the original claim, diagnose the first missing dependency; preserve the unmet goal and identify the limited evidence actually available.
methods.limits: Synthetic error histograms support distribution analysis only; they do not establish waveform evolution, convergence from raw resolutions or a newly generated catalog.

methods.title: Molecular graph construction and architecture comparisons
